“Large demonstrations do not inevitably descend into rioting or looting, but the pattern seen in recent weeks — whereby initially peaceful protests have at times been joined or exploited by more confrontational groups — means that further damaging unrest cannot be ruled out,” said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

Such risks aren’t new in France, though the economic loss has been rising in recent years. The Gilets Jaunes protests of 2018-19 resulted in about €220 million in insured losses, according to Morningstar. The riots of June 2023 generated some €730 million in insured losses. It is not yet clear what the latest protests will end up costing.

The unrest has “prompted further discussions around the need for French government reinsurance solutions to cover future SRCC events", Humphries of Allianz said.

France this year approved the creation of a state-backed fund to provide mandatory riot coverage in property policies for all businesses and homeowners across the country. The fund is expected to go into effect in January and will be financed by contributions levied on insurers, as well as a 0.8% increase in premiums paid by policyholders, Alvarez says. Insurers will retain 10% of the loss exposure.

“It ensures they still have skin in the game,” he said.

title: Chinese coal buyers balk at Indonesian miners’ contract demands
article:
(Nov 10): Chinese coal buyers are pushing back against attempts by some Indonesian miners to rewrite 2027 supply contracts in ways that would shift the risk of government-driven disruptions onto customers, threatening to delay deals that underpin decisions on output.

Some Indonesian producers are seeking waiver clauses that would release them from obligations to deliver contracted volumes if Jakarta cuts output quotas or delays export approvals, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Chinese buyers are reluctant to accept such provisions, particularly after changes in government policy contributed to disruptions in deliveries this year, said the people, asking not to be named discussing confidential contract terms.

Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, is exerting greater control over output and exports of the fossil fuel to safeguard supplies for domestic power production. Miners must meet local obligations before they can go ahead with overseas sales while the government is also routing exports through state-controlled channels to improve pricing transparency and curb practices such as under-invoicing.

As a result, Indonesian coal exports to China are down almost 10% in the first 10 months from a year earlier, according to data from Kpler. That’s even as overall production is forecast to be around 720 million tonnes this year, ahead of the government’s initial target of 600 million tonnes.

The changes in Indonesia, under the so-called RKAB work plan and budget system that seeks to control mining production volumes, are complicating negotiations with customers.

Some Chinese traders are delaying annual contract talks as they wait for greater clarity on Jakarta’s production target and the allocation of individual mining quotas, according to analysts who cover the sector, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter. Further delays could mean that producers enter the new year without certainty over how much coal they are authorised to mine.

See also: US seeks deeper Myanmar ties, access to ‘bountiful’ rare earths

The policy shifts may be more disruptive for contracts with overseas customers than production. Indonesia will probably keep output at about 700 million tonnes next year, so an export supply squeeze is unlikely, said Glen Kurokawa, an analyst at CRU Group.

Delayed contracts and broad waiver clauses could leave individual Chinese buyers uncertain whether nominated supplies will be delivered, however. That could increase their exposure to spot-price volatility and potentially push demand toward Indonesia’s competitors including Australia and Mongolia.

title: Zara owner backs new fund targeting supply chain emissions
article:
(Nov 10): Inditex SA is backing a fund set up to grant low-cost loans to suppliers that invest in energy efficiency, as the fashion industry faces pressure to cut its carbon footprint.

In a private-public partnership that chief executive officer Óscar García Maceiras says is the first of its kind, the world’s biggest fashion retailer has committed US$50 million to the fund, which is led by the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank’s private-sector arm. IFC plans to raise US$400 million to help small companies transition to net-zero business models.

As much as 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions come from the textile industry, according to United Nations estimates. At the same time, many suppliers are located in developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to weather extremes associated with rising temperatures. Suppliers in such markets need access to funds to pay for better machinery and cheaper, renewable energy has eluded to help them adapt.

Emissions are “connected with all of the processes” contained within the fashion industry’s supply chain, García Maceiras said in an interview. “That’s why supporting the transformation of the suppliers — in terms of water consumption, use of chemicals, waste or the implementation of renewable energies — is key.”

The fund’s launch comes as nations gather at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye to address a US$1.3 trillion goal for climate finance to developing countries. As host country, Türkiye launched the Climate Implementation Bridge in September in order to turn climate commitments into concrete projects.

García Maceiras said that when it comes to textile-related emissions, a collective initiative from the industry is required, in part because suppliers often work with many retailers. As an investor in the fund, Inditex aims to serve as “a catalyst” to bring in other companies, he said.

See also: Vodacom profit jumps 26% as Safaricom gains boost earnings

“This is not an Inditex fund; it’s open to the industry as a whole,” he said. The goal is to “demonstrate that with the involvement of different players within the textile industry, we could reach the objective of the transformation of the whole industry.”

The small and medium-sized suppliers “at the heart of global brand supply chains need access to affordable, appropriately structured financing to stay competitive,” Sarvesh Suri, the IFC’s regional vice president for Asia and the Pacific, said in a statement.

The fund, which will be managed by impact investor Social Investment Managers & Advisors LLC, will help close the climate finance gap by providing loans both to textile makers and to the energy companies they use, according to a joint statement published on Tuesday. Eligible companies may also seek free technical advice on switching to renewable energy sources, to make machinery more energy and water efficient, and reducing chemical use.

See also: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals

Other investors in the fund include the US-based Global Environment Facility and the Apparel Impact Institute, the Dutch development bank FMO, French development financier Proparco and British International Investment. The first close is expected to reach $225 million, with more rounds planned to achieve the target goal.

“The success of the fund and the involvement of relevant institutions could open the door for additional, similar initiatives that could reach a wide range of different suppliers,” García Maceiras said.

Inditex’s participation follows more than two years of work at the company to identify the investments suppliers might need to make in order to reduce emissions and other environmental impacts. It’s part of the retailer’s effort to cut its own environmental footprint while maintaining growth.

“The idea is to reduce the total emissions of the group while maintaining the expected growth that we have been achieving consistently year after year,” García Maceiras said. “By 2030, our aim is to reduce up to 53% of our total emissions. At the end of 2025, we reached 11%.”

title: Vodacom profit jumps 26% as Safaricom gains boost earnings
article:
(Nov 10): Vodacom Group Ltd’s half-year headline profit jumped 26% as the company battles to keep control of Safaricom Plc, which boosted the wireless carrier’s earnings during the period.

Vodacom’s so-called headline earnings per share — which exclude one-time gains — climbed to 5.87 rand for the six months ended Sept 30 from 4.67 rand a year earlier.

The firm declared an interim dividend of 3.55 rand, 7.6% higher than a year earlier. Customers increased 12% to a record 250 million.

The Johannesburg-based company that’s majority-owned by the UK’s Vodafone Group Plc, booked a fair-value gain after it remeasured its stake in East Africa’s biggest telecommunications firm.

The increase follows Vodacom’s move to take control of Safaricom after it completed the purchase of an additional 20% interest in June, lifting its effective stake in the Kenyan company to 55%.

That holding is now subject to a legal battle in the country, with the High Court last month declaring the government’s sale of a 15% holding to Vodacom unconstitutional and ordering the shares returned to the state. An appeals court has since allowed Vodacom to retain the shares while fast-tracking an appeal of the ruling.

See also: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals

title: TSMC’s revenue rises 60% in a sign of resilient AI chip demand
article:
(Nov 10): Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co posted a 60% increase in monthly sales, reflecting the company’s central role in a global AI infrastructure build-out.

The go-to chipmaker for Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc reported October revenue of NT$586.9 billion. That pace was up from around 51% for the September quarter. Analysts on average are projecting 63% growth for the year’s final three months.

Taiwan’s largest company last month delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook, sustaining a torrid pace of growth in the post-ChatGPT era. Yet investors continue to grapple with the longer-term outlook for AI demand, given the rising cost of financing expensive and resource-hungry data centres. TSMC’s shares have gyrated alongside the rest of the tech sector, buffeted by fears that the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms may lead to tougher oversight of the artificial intelligence sector.

TSMC — a key barometer for the industry because it makes chips for a broad swathe of tech players — is betting on a fundamental shift. It is trying to build and furnish about 20 factories at home and overseas, an unprecedented pace for a company that typically works on four or five new buildings simultaneously.

CEO C C Wei has stressed, though, that it remains in prudent expansion mode, exploring a new manufacturing site in Texas while discussing a potential tie-up with Elon Musk’s Terafab chipmaking endeavour.

See also: Japan’s Rapidus is said likely to miss mass production deadline

The company has so far managed to accelerate sales growth and ramped up capacity expansion. The company reiterated its capital expenditures will reach as much as US$64 billion, a record, this year.

title: Rising fuel flows through Hormuz may help ease strained market
article:
(Nov 10): The volume of refined products being loaded within the Persian Gulf is rising, with most of that exiting the Strait of Hormuz and providing some relief to one of the tightest corners of the global oil market nine months into the Iran war.

The region loaded about three million barrels a day of distillates, including diesel, petrochemical feedstock naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas, in October, according to data from ship-tracking and analytics firm Vortexa Ltd. While that is still only about half of pre-conflict levels, that is up from a trough in May of about one million barrels a day.

Most of those shipments have or will soon exit through Hormuz, said Xavier Tang, senior market analyst for Vortexa, although exact volumes are hard to pin down due to transfers within the Gulf and methods of obfuscating flows such as vessels turning off their transponders. Still, the recovery in oil products is lagging that for crude, which at some points in prior months had neared early-February levels.

“Crude is going at about 80% to 85% of pre-war levels” including pipeline exports, while “products are at about 35% to 40%,” Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of industry consultant FGE NexantECA, said last week, referring to Middle Eastern oil exports including through Hormuz.

There’s been an overall pickup in vessel traffic across different commodities in the crucial waterway. Crude remains the most successful at exiting the embattled region, while flows of liquefied natural gas have risen to about a third of levels before the conflict.

See also: Oil extends drop as Trump says further Iran strikes unnecessary

“Oil infrastructure such as refineries remains susceptible to drone strikes,” which has led the region’s producers to prioritise crude shipments, Tang said.

Global refined markets remain tight, with some countries opting to prioritise local consumption despite attractive profits on exports. International shipments of diesel from major producer China, for example, may remain curbed as the country grapples with low domestic inventories.

title: Copper extends rebound as global technology stocks resume rally
article:
(Nov 10): Copper extended its rebound from last week’s slump, tracking a rally in technology shares due to the metal’s use in power infrastructure and data centres.

The industrial metal has moved in tandem with artificial intelligence stocks in recent months. It had slumped 2.7% to a three-month low last week as concerns rose that the Democrats’ sweep of US midterm elections could mean greater regulation of AI.

Stocks advanced on Tuesday (Nov 10), with South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index the top performer in the region. In China, the market was hit by a supply squeeze that’s driving a rapid surge in spot premiums to record levels.

The tightness has started to bring in more imported cargoes as traders aim to take advantage of an arbitrage window to bring in metal from overseas at a profit, Jinrui Futures Co said in a note.

Investors were also monitoring a major shortage in the global aluminium market fuelled by declining stockpiles of the crucial industrial commodity. Buyers are facing rising prices for spot metal and there is little immediate prospect of relief before new shipments from Indonesia arrive.

Copper rose 0.3% to US$13,937 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 10.52am in Shanghai. Aluminium slipped 0.3% to US$3,058.50 while other metals edged higher. Iron ore was down 0.2% at US$92.55 a tonne in Singapore.

See also: Asian rice price climbs near two-year high in inflation threat

title: Japan’s Rapidus is said likely to miss mass production deadline
article:
(Nov 10): Japanese government-backed startup Rapidus Corp has fallen behind schedule on its high-stakes pledge to mass produce cutting-edge chips by March 2028 and may no longer be able to make that deadline.

The startup, which has received billions of dollars’ worth of public funds, has yet to successfully produce a key type of advanced memory that is an essential component of all processors, people familiar with the matter said. Rapidus has yet to produce functioning static random access memory cells, or SRAM, a critical step that needed to be completed by the summer to manufacture 2nm chips in time, they said.

Engineers are under intense pressure to pick up the pace but the failure to meet that technological milestone means the company is at least months behind schedule, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public.

A significant delay may jeopardise public support for Rapidus, widely viewed as a long-shot attempt to build a top-tier foundry from scratch and lower Japan’s advanced chip reliance on Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Dust and particle control within the cleanroom remains another issue the company is working to resolve, the people said.

The government has so far officially earmarked more than ¥2 trillion in state funding to Rapidus. Severe technological issues could also push back Rapidus’s goal of going public by 2032.

“Rapidus continues to devote its full efforts toward the start of mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027,” a spokesperson said in an email. The company declined to provide details about its technological development, which it said is confidential. In September, a panel of outside experts commissioned by a government agency reported the company’s development is progressing, it said.

See also: TSMC said to mull making advanced AI memory chips

Last month, Rapidus chairman Tetsuro Higashi said the venture was on track for mass production as scheduled, without elaborating.

Advanced logic chips require hundreds of millions of embedded SRAM cells. Manufacturers need to reproduce each of these cells, including their transistors, at atomic-scale precision to prevent operational failures and ensure stable data retention. At the nanometre scale, even a minor microscopic deviation can cause debilitating chip failures.

Rapidus will continue to pursue 2nm manufacturing and may ultimately succeed after some years’ delay, the people said. Rapidus seeks to compete against Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which is building facilities in the US, Intel Corp and Samsung Electronics Co. All are racing to develop manufacturing processes and meet artificial intelligence service providers’ voracious demand for increasingly powerful chips.

See also: OpenAI’s Altman meets Samsung executives as chip crunch deepens

After launching its pilot production line at its factory in Hokkaido, northern Japan, Rapidus said in July last year that it successfully manufactured functioning transistors — an early step toward making cutting-edge chips. Since then, technological progress has consisted mainly of process design kit releases.

Last month, Economy Minister Ryosei Akazawa said the government was ready to continue supporting Rapidus until the venture becomes financially viable, given the importance of cutting-edge chips for Japan’s economic security. Since Rapidus’ creation in 2022, TSMC has built a plant in southern Japan, with plans to build another factory that will manufacture 3nm chips.

In September, independent director Yoshimitsu Kobayashi told Bloomberg News that Rapidus is targeting mass production with a yield of at least 80%, or four out of every five chips produced. CEO Atsuyoshi Koike, who has floated plans to build two additional factories in Hokkaido and a plant on the moon, and representative director Atsuo Shimizu have said that Kobayashi’s definition is not shared by all executives.

title: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals
article:
(Nov 10): Citigroup Inc chief executive officer Jane Fraser said a securities licence in China completes the bank’s product offering there and gives it an edge over competitors.

“All I would say to the competition is watch out, because we have this unique offering already from that global network, the history we’ve got, and now with this,” Fraser said to Bloomberg Television in Shanghai.

After a five-year wait, the lender last month received a approval for the licence to run a securities business in mainland China, far later than many of its competitors.

The firm’s path has been fraught with delays. Since applying in late 2021, the bank has had to navigate shifting Chinese data-security rules and scrutiny from US regulators.

The license lets the bank raise capital, trade and get better access to investors, Fraser said. It also lets Citigroup connect investors between the world and China, she said.

Kaleem Rizvi, global co-head of corporate banking, said in an interview from Shanghai that the firm envisions hiring about 100 bankers over the next several years after it won approval for the licence.

See also: European Investment Bank’s Calvino says US turmoil is driving capital to Europe

As for the AI market, Fraser said that last week’s selloff was a tad overdone, with hedge funds taking money off the table. She said the need for compute is not going away and called the AI buildout a multiyear effort, though not everyone will be a winner.

“When you have innovation at that speed, you need to have risk management at that speed,” Fraser said.

Citigroup reported a record third quarter, Fraser said, with growth across its business lines.

See also: BMW widens battery component suppliers with Samsung, LG Energy

For 2027, she said the aim is to diversify the businesses for all seasons so the bank can support clients as they transform and grow. She said she would love a year a little more boring than 2026.

title: Singapore extends GST waiver to activities related to wholesale gold transactions
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Ministry of Finance (MOF) will be extending the GST waiver to specified wholesale investment precious metal (IPM) related services between institutional participants covered by the existing GST framework. These services include activities such as vaulting, refining, recasting, assaying, and broking.

The initiative seeks to support the growth of wholesale Loco Singapore gold market activities where the gold traded is not for domestic consumption. This enhanced tax framework is expected to take effect from April 2027, with further details to be announced at Budget 2027.

Under the current Approved Refiner and Consolidator Scheme, GST is waived on IPM-related goods supplied between approved refiners and consolidators for refining activities, to ease their cashflow and compliance.The existing framework also exempts the import and local supply of IPM from GST.

Deputy prime minister and MAS chairman Gan Kim Yong thinks the enhanced GST framework will both facilitate the trading of gold and central bank storage of gold in Singapore. He adds: “I have to emphasise that this is a transaction between institutions and the wholesale trade, and it's not targeted at the consumer retail market. So that is why the GST framework is built on that basis.”

Speaking at a media doorstop, Gan also announced that MAS is launching its central bank gold vaulting service. “Given an increasingly uncertain external environment, demand for gold as an asset class is rising as investors and central banks look for resilience and diversification,” says Gan. “Foreign central banks and sovereign entities now have an additional sovereign custody option in Singapore for their gold reserves.”

Besides offering an alternative storage option, the service also provides secure, allocated custody, reliable servicing and efficient access to gold-market liquidity during Asian trading hours, notes MAS.

See also: Central banks buy gold at fastest pace since 2024, WGC says

Under this development, MAS will store up to 500 tonnes of gold in its national currency vault, with room for expansion as demand grows. MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to these institutions.

Gan says that the development of Singapore’s gold market is a “natural extension” to Singapore’s role as a trusted financial centre and will anchor new high-value activities across trading, risk management, custody, and professional services in the city-state.

“By connecting secure storage with trading and settlement, we are building a market where gold can be held, managed and traded in Singapore,” he adds. “It will create good jobs and capabilities, while adding depth and resilience to our financial sector, strengthening Singapore’s role as a trusted connector between Asia and global gold markets.”

See also: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide

Gan also shared that Singapore’s gold clearing system will be ready by end-2026, with live trading and liquidity building up from the first quarter next year. In June, DBS, Deutsche Bank, ICBC Standard Bank, JP Morgan, OCBC, and UOB signed a memorandum of understanding with SGX Group to develop an over-the-counter gold clearing system,

MAS announced that industry testing of the clearing system has been completed and the clearing system rulebook will be finalised soon. Live trading and market operations are expected to commence in 1Q 2027, with gold market liquidity building throughout the year.

JP Morgan senior country officer Wai Mei Hong says, “We are pleased to work with SGX Group in advancing Singapore’s OTC gold clearing system. As global demand for gold grows, this initiative will strengthen Singapore’s role as a trading hub, deepen liquidity across time zones and help us better serve clients.”

UOB head of group global markets Kelvin Ng says that the combination of vaulting, enhanced tax support for wholesale gold activities and a gold clearing ecosystem will create "stronger foundations" for market growth. “These developments will deepen liquidity, improve price discovery and reinforce Singapore's role as a key precious metals centre serving the Asia-Pacific region,” adds Ng.

In addition, it was also announced that SGX is targeting to launch its physically deliverable gold kilobar futures in the second quarter of 2027.

title: Australia to create AI safety regulator, mandatory safety rules
article:
(Nov 10): Australia will create a new artificial intelligence (AI) safety regulator that will have the power to impose “significant penalties” on companies that do the wrong thing, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday in Canberra.

The government is in the process of writing AI-related legislation, with the new regulator to be included in those bills, Albanese said at a press conference. Firms will need to provide mandatory notifications of any security incidents to the government and allow independent evaluation of their models, he added.

The issue of AI safety was brought to the fore in September when it was revealed that an OpenAI model had hacked an Australian government website. While the information accessed wasn’t sensitive personal data, the attack on a government website shone a spotlight on such risks.

That followed a series of incidents in which OpenAI models broke into online resources of outside companies, most notably with the case of Hugging Face, a website hosting AI datasets.

Australia established a review in response to the hacking. It recommended changes including reforming criminal laws so that the government can criminally punish “egregious regulatory non-compliance” and create a “failure to prevent” offence where a company creates a model and doesn’t take reasonable steps to stop it from doing harm.

The government will accept all of the review’s recommendations, Albanese said.

See also: Why Singapore's next AI question is value, not just spend

title: Singapore’s interbank rate hits highest in more than a year
article:
(Nov 10): Singapore’s benchmark interest rate climbed to the highest level in more than a year on tighter local liquidity and expectations for further US interest-rate hikes.

The cost of overnight borrowing in Singapore’s interbank market rose 11.7 basis points to 1.7446% as of Friday, according to data published Tuesday. That was the highest since July 2025. Local markets were shut on Monday for a holiday.

Singapore’s borrowing costs are largely influenced by global interest rates and currency expectations because the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy through the exchange rate. That leaves local rates sensitive to shifts in US monetary policy, with markets bracing for the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening after a 25-basis-point hike in September.

Liquidity in Singapore has also tightened as loan growth outpaced deposits. The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 69.8% in September, the highest since August 2024, from 65.8% at the end of last year, according to the latest central bank data.

“Liquidity appears on the tight side recently, while the long weekend might have added to the tightness,” said Frances Cheung, head of foreign exchange and rates strategy at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.

See also: ‘Longer-term measures’ being studied to strengthen transparency, trust in real estate industry: Sun Xueling

Cheung said compounded SORA rates, while lagging, “provide a better picture of the broader trend”. The three-month rate is moving towards around 1.4%, in line with her long-held expectation for around year-end, she said.

The three-month compounded SORA was at 1.3413% on Friday.

title: Nvidia intervened in US probe of Megaspeed chip smuggling
article:
(Nov 10): Nvidia Corp’s general counsel intervened in a US government probe of suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, questioning whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining an executive from the Singapore-based firm who’s now at the heart of a scandal threatening Jensen Huang.

In late summer 2025, Nvidia’s Tim Teter called Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees US chip export curbs, to ask about the Megaspeed investigation, according to people familiar with the matter.

Specifically, Teter wanted to know whether Kessler’s Bureau of Industry and Security was involved in the Singapore government’s recent detention of Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, according to the people. Singapore police had brought Alice in for questioning and restricted her from leaving the country. BIS was not involved in that action, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity owing to the sensitivity of the matter.

Jensen on Sunday admitted to having an affair with Alice after previously lying about the nature of their relationship, which is now the subject of an investigation by Nvidia’s board. An Nvidia spokesperson said that Teter was unaware of the affair at the time he called Kessler about Alice’s detention in Singapore.

It’s unclear whether Teter made any specific requests of Kessler related to his agency’s investigation into Megaspeed, which was separate from Singapore’s. But in the weeks that followed, BIS staff were muzzled in their ability to look into the company, including a mandate that they route all requests of Nvidia through Kessler or seek his approval for outreach — a highly unusual step that remains unique to the chipmaker, the people said. They were also told not to mention Megaspeed or Speedmatrix, the company’s Malaysian subsidiary, in external communications.

Teter, meanwhile, reached out directly to the agency’s staff, including requesting a meeting with one of them, according to some of the people. That BIS employee declined the meeting, and Teter responded that he didn’t understand why his request was spurned, since Kessler had granted him permission to communicate with BIS employees. It’s unclear exactly what Teter wanted to discuss with these individuals.

See also: Nvidia shares drop after CEO Huang’s affair triggers board probe

The employees forwarded the email to Kessler, who told them hours later to continue handling the case by the book, to which the employees responded: “10-4. Thank you.” Kessler didn’t otherwise weigh in on how the employees should proceed with the case, according to one of the people. The New York Times reported earlier on Teter’s outreach to BIS employees and their exchange with Kessler.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson for the agency said. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.”

In late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working on the case with BIS — standard practice for any BIS investigation that turns into a criminal probe — requested that BIS pause its efforts, the people said. BIS has not made any progress since then, despite the agency having enough evidence to move forward.

See also: Anthropic buys power for AI data centres in US$3.4 bil deal, FT says

It’s an extraordinary episode that raises questions about Nvidia’s ability to influence US investigations into breaches of China chip curbs, as well as what exactly Teter sought to do with any additional information about Alice’s detention in Singapore.

An Nvidia spokesperson, asked about the company’s intervention in BIS’s Megaspeed probe, said that Nvidia consults with government officials “to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups.”

“We work to resolve any allegations of ‘diversion’ promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide,” the spokesperson said. “Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding US policy and hurt American economic and national security.”

Despite that stance, in the months after Teter’s initial call with Kessler, Nvidia gave BIS an incomplete account of its business with Megaspeed. After several visits to Megaspeed’s data centers — 12 facilities owned by eight companies across three countries in Southeast Asia — Nvidia had sent inventory checks to the agency and declared to Bloomberg News in mid-November 2025 that everything was where it should be.

The company also said at the time that it had asked the US government whether it needed to cut off business with Megaspeed, and was told no.

But Nvidia’s tabulations, as relayed to the US government, undercounted the number of chips it had sold to Megaspeed via hardware partners by 50,000 units, according to trade records analysed by Bloomberg. That’s worth billions of dollars. After being pressed about the gap, Nvidia told Bloomberg in December 2025 that it had checked additional Megaspeed warehouses that contained the missing hardware, while declining to state exactly how many chips it found in those facilities or provide any further details.

Nvidia also declined to comment on significant additional discrepancies in Megaspeed’s data centre footprint, including that two of the eight data centre operators Nvidia told officials in Washington it had visited said they did not, in fact, have Megaspeed’s hardware — and that Megaspeed boasts something of a Chinese corporate twin. It’s unclear whether Nvidia has communicated with BIS or DOJ on these topics.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Since then, the largest of Megaspeed’s data centre landlords dropped Megaspeed as a tenant. Nvidia, for its part, has consistently declined to comment on whether it has completed any additional visits to that site or any of Megaspeed’s other facilities, despite pledging to do so nearly a year ago.

BIS, meanwhile, has declined to impose restrictions on Nvidia’s ability to do business with the firm despite calls for such a step from senior levels of the Trump administration. Megaspeed has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations, and said that its outreach to the US government about the probe has gone unanswered.

The company added that Singapore’s investigation “into activities related to alleged chip diversion concluded earlier this year with no adverse action against Megaspeed.” Bloomberg has been unable to reach Alice Huang despite repeated attempts over the past year. Megaspeed was not speaking on her behalf.

Around three months ago, Nvidia’s Teter had a call with someone else on Trump’s team — an official at the White House. He told this official, according to a person familiar with the call, that Alice is not as important in Megaspeed as she makes herself out to be, a likely reference to her statement on LinkedIn that she is the company’s CEO even though she doesn’t hold and has never held that role on paper. Still, because of the bad publicity surrounding Alice, Teter continued, Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed.

That bad publicity began in October 2025, when The New York Times first reported that the US government was looking into the company. In November 2025, Malaysian trade records show, Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia’s GB300s processors, at the time the most advanced and sought after AI chips on the market, worth some US$787 million.

Today, Megaspeed remains an official Nvidia Cloud Partner — a coveted designation in the data centre world that Nvidia generally takes away from companies when they no longer do business with those firms.

title: Oil extends drop as Trump says further Iran strikes unnecessary
article:
(Nov 10): Oil extended declines from the lowest close since August after US President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary.

Brent dropped below US$92 a barrel after sliding almost 6% on Monday, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$86. Hopes for an earlier end to the war with Iran have grown since the US midterm elections, with congressional Democrats weighing whether to use a Dec 11 government shutdown deadline to pressure Trump to end the conflict, now in its ninth month.

The president said the US remains “locked and loaded”, while signalling he’s looking to wind down the conflict after the midterm results underscored its unpopularity. “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” he told reporters on Monday after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House. Qatar is a mediator in talks between the US and Iran.

Brent has tumbled from a six-month high at the end of October. Last week, the global benchmark notched its biggest weekly decline since April 2020 when not adjusted for expiry. However, it’s not yet clear whether the softer rhetoric will translate into tangible progress towards ending the war started by the US and Israel, with political uncertainty deepening after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost his parliamentary majority at the end of last month.

“The midterm results have significantly narrowed Trump’s options for a large-scale, long-term military operation against Iran and that’s reflected in his rhetoric,” said Takahiro Asaoka, senior economist at Itochu Research Institute Inc. That’s taking some of the geopolitical premium out of oil, although Brent will likely stay above US$85 a barrel without a deal with Tehran, he added.

Months of on-and-off negotiations have failed to produce a resolution. Tehran has insisted that the US end its naval blockade of the country’s ports and lift sanctions, while Washington is pressing Iran to stop attacking vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and make concessions over its nuclear programme.

See also: Oil extends rebound on uncertainty over Iran war peace progress

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down the chances of a breakthrough in talks with Iran, while risks to energy infrastructure remain. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was targeted Monday in the Medina region, causing a limited fire that was extinguished, the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported.

Geopolitical risks elsewhere also remain in focus. Ukraine continued to strike Russian refineries, while Moscow repeatedly targeted energy and civilian infrastructure in its neighbour. US-mediated talks between the sides are due to start Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, and the presence of higher-level diplomats than in previous rounds has been seen as a sign of greater openness to substantive negotiations after months of stalemate.

Traders this week will also watch monthly market reports from all three major forecasting agencies: the US Energy Information Administration on Tuesday, Opec on Wednesday and the International Energy Agency on Friday.

See also: Oil extends slide after plunging 8% on hopes to end US-Iran war
• Brent for January settlement dropped 0.8% to US$91.80 a barrel at 9.58am in Singapore.

title: Asian stocks climb as tech rallies, oil slips
article:
(Nov 10): Asian stocks advanced, tracking Wall Street higher as a rally in technology shares and a further decline in oil prices boosted risk sentiment.

South Korea’s Kospi Index jumped 3.9% to lead gains in the region, followed by Japan’s Nikkei 225 and Taiwan’s benchmark. A broader gauge of Asian equities climbed 2%, while futures for US benchmarks were little changed.

On Monday, the S&P 500 rallied the most since April 8. A gauge of chipmakers surged nearly 7% while the Nasdaq 100 ended 3.4% higher. That came even as shares of Nvidia Corp slid 4.3% amid a probe into chief executive officer Jensen Huang after his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.

Elsewhere, Brent crude slipped further on Tuesday after slumping almost 6% to settle below US$93 a barrel in the previous session. President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary but the US remains “locked and loaded”, an indication that he’s winding down the conflict.

The rally in stocks follows a tumultuous week during which chipmakers were sold off on concerns that the Democratic sweep of US Congress in the midterms would spur tighter regulation of the artificial intelligence industry. Meanwhile, a steady decline in oil has helped temper inflation fears.

“The sharp drop in oil prices has given markets some much-needed breathing room,” said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone Group. “Investors are also buying back into stocks after last week’s brutal selloff. We still need to see whether buying interest can hold up.”

See also: Asia hedge funds, rich investors face big losses in AI rout

Anthropic PBC can begin formally marketing its much-anticipated IPO as early as Tuesday, enabling it to make the case to investors that now is the right time to go public despite last week’s swoon in AI-related stocks.

The recent tech selloff represented a reset rather than the start of a structural downturn in the AI investment cycle. But the rebound does not remove the risks created by concentrated positioning and elevated expectations, said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

On the economic front, investors will be watching October US consumer prices data, which is slated to be released Tuesday and is expected to show smaller increases than in September.

See also: Watch for the double top pattern that precedes a market crash

“We continue to see economic conditions as supportive of corporate fundamentals,” said Brock Weimer at Edward Jones. “Thus, we recommend that investors maintain an overweight allocation to equities relative to fixed income.”

title: Canada expands US tariff exemptions, cuts some aluminium relief
article:
(Nov 10): Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is changing the rules for importers, allowing them to apply for exemptions from Canadian tariffs on a wider range of US goods while ending relief on some American-made aluminum products.

When US President Donald Trump began imposing tariffs on Canadian goods in March 2025, Canada responded with retaliatory levies. But Carney’s government allowed importers to request “remission” from the tariffs in some circumstances — for example, if they’re buying essential products from the US that are hard to find elsewhere.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Monday the government will now extend tariff relief for “non-steel goods” made in the US and used in Canadian mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction, as well as some other items.

Companies in those categories will be eligible for tariff remission until June 30, 2028.

The remission program is already so broad that most of the counter-tariffs Canada applies on US shipments haven’t actually resulted in revenue for the government.

From March 2025 through October 26, 2026, Canada assessed C$14.1 billion (US$10 billion) worth of tariffs on products from the US. But C$8.9 billion was “remitted or relieved” to mitigate the hit to Canada, leaving net revenue of C$5.2 billion, according to a disclosure last week by the government.

See also: Vietnam turns to taxes, state borrowing to finance growth push

Products used by some public health, education, safety and national security organizations also will be exempt from tariffs until June 2028, the government said Monday.

At the same time, Champagne also announced the end of tariff remission on a list of other products to encourage purchases from Canadian manufacturers.

Tariff relief will no longer be available on some US-made trailers as of Dec 1, nor on types of aluminum wire, pipes, tubes, or some paperboard products, from Feb 1, 2027. That’s “to incentivize the use of domestic inputs,” the Department of Finance said in a statement.

See also: Asia’s innovation capacity is improving but could be better

Canada doubled counter-tariffs on many US aluminium products to 50% on Sept 8, while still allowing Canadian buyers to request relief. Some Canadian aluminium manufacturers, already facing export challenges due to hefty US duties, have said that the remission programme leaves them at a disadvantage in pursuing domestic sales.

“By adjusting our tariff relief measures, we are helping our businesses staying competitive, encouraging the use of Canadian-made goods, and protecting our industries and workers most impacted by the unfair US tariffs,” Champagne said in the statement.

title: Climate investing’s next challenge: Identifying the companies ready to transition
article:
A portfolio can become cleaner on paper without the companies in it becoming any better prepared for a lower-carbon economy. Investors are increasingly weighing not just how much companies emit, but how well they can adapt and what that means for long-term investment risks and opportunities.

The distinction matters in a region where energy, manufacturing and other emissions-intensive industries play important economic roles. Companies with high emissions today may be investing heavily to transform their operations, while those with smaller carbon footprints are not necessarily better prepared for future policy, technology and market changes.

This approach is already taking shape in institutional portfolios. In 2025, Aware Super, one of Australia’s largest superannuation funds with more than A$235 billion ($210.84 billion) in assets, adopted a transition-based carbon reduction benchmark developed with MSCI for more than A$50 billion in public equities, bringing companies’ transition progress alongside their existing emissions into its investment framework.

“The industry has moved beyond portfolio optics to capital allocation with intent,” says Shane Edwards, head of Asia Pacific at MSCI. “Rather than simply excluding higher-emitting companies to lower a portfolio’s reported carbon footprint, investors are staying invested in companies with a credible path to lower emissions, because that is genuinely where engagement and capital can shift outcomes.”

Lowering a portfolio's reported emissions and investing in companies that are decarbonizing are not necessarily the same thing.

Some of the largest opportunities for emissions reductions lie in industries with the highest carbon footprints. Excluding these companies outright can mean overlooking businesses making credible progress.

But identifying them is not straightforward. Corporate targets alone reveal little about whether companies have the plans, resources or ability to deliver on their commitments.

That distinction is influencing how some institutional investors approach climate benchmarks.

“A company's current carbon footprint only tells part of the story,” says Agnes Hong, head of public market equities at Aware Super. “We wanted an approach that also captures where a business is heading and whether management is taking credible steps to position the company for a lower-carbon economy.”

The challenge is not simply deciding which companies are better prepared for the transition. It is determining how those assessments should affect portfolio weights without compromising diversification, risk controls or investment objectives.

“The transition to a lower-carbon economy will require significant change across many industries,” Hong says. “A forward-looking framework allows us to recognise companies making credible progress, even when they operate in sectors that have traditionally been viewed as emissions intensive.”

Singapore’s regulatory expectations are evolving along similar lines. Transition planning guidelines issued by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in March 2026 call on banks, insurers and asset managers to strengthen their forward-looking assessments of transition and physical risks, alongside engagement with investee companies.1

The implications extend to portfolio construction. More detailed assessments of companies’ transition readiness can inform investment decisions, but changes to benchmark weights can also affect sector exposures, diversification and tracking error. Asset owners face the task of balancing these considerations with their investment mandates and long-term performance objectives.

“Members expect us to take climate risk seriously, but they also expect us to remain disciplined investors,” says Hong. “Any climate framework we adopt must be capable of being implemented at scale, measured rigorously and justified through the lens of long-term member outcomes.”

The challenge becomes more complex across large portfolios managed by multiple investment teams. Consistent data, transparent methodologies and governance are essential to applying climate considerations without materially altering a portfolio's underlying risk and return characteristics.

“The market is already pricing transition risk, whether investors are ready for that or not,” says Edwards. “We have seen real repricing as capital moves toward companies with business models built for the transition, not simply those with the best-stated climate targets.”

Transition readiness is only part of the picture. Physical climate hazards can also affect company operations, supply chains and asset values, introducing risks that may not be apparent from company-level disclosures.

For Southeast Asian investors, this is particularly relevant given the region's concentration of manufacturing facilities, ports and infrastructure exposed to floods, extreme heat and severe storms.

Understanding where these risks are concentrated can help investors assess companies' capacity to adapt and strengthen resilience across regional and global supply chains.

“Location-specific insight is increasingly important for investors trying to get a real read on physical risk, which doesn’t live at a company’s headquarters, but wherever that company actually operates: the factory, the port, the warehouse,” says Edwards.

MSCI tracks 4.5 million operational locations across 780,000 companies against 31 physical climate hazards. Combining geospatial data with AI and other analytical techniques can help investors assess exposures that broader company-level measures may miss.

“Wildfires, floods and severe storms are already disrupting operations today, with an estimated US$1.3 trillion ($1.66 trillion) in financial exposure on the table,” Edwards says.

Such analysis can reveal where climate-related disruptions could affect individual businesses and how those exposures accumulate across a portfolio. It can also inform decisions about risk management, diversification and capital allocation.

Investors now have more information to assess not only where companies stand on emissions, but how prepared they are for the transition and the risks that could affect their operations.

“Setting climate goals is relatively straightforward,” says Hong. “The real challenge is translating those goals into portfolio construction decisions across tens of billions of dollars of assets while maintaining consistency, transparency and investment discipline.”

Aware Super's experience illustrates what that takes. Reliable data, robust methodologies and coordination across investment teams to incorporate climate considerations while managing diversification and tracking error.

For institutional investors, climate considerations cannot sit apart from the wider investment process. The growing availability of forward-looking data offers a more informed basis for assessing which companies are adapting, where risks remain and how those assessments should influence portfolio allocations.

The next phase of climate investing is not simply about meeting emissions targets, but using those insights to make investment decisions that account for both the risks of transition and the opportunities in companies helping to drive the region’s next phase of economic growth.

1Monetary Authority of Singapore, “MAS Sets Supervisory Expectations on Financial Institutions for Transition Planning Practices in Addressing Environmental Risk,” March 5, 2026.

For more on how MSCI and Aware Super worked together to develop a transition-focused benchmark, read the full story here.

title: SoftBank, Grab and PETROS lock in US$1.85 bil seed capital for AI infrastructure in Malaysia
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 9): SoftBank Group Corp, Grab Holdings Ltd and Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (PETROS) have agreed on plans for US$1.85 billion in initial combined seed capital to build AI infrastructure across Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia in partnership with global hyperscalers.

Of the proposed initial investment of US$1.85 billion, US$1 billion will be invested in Sarawak and the other US$850 million in Peninsula Malaysia.

Building on the framework agreement signed in Kuching, Malaysia, on Oct 8, 2026, the three companies signed a joint development agreement (JDA), marking the next phase of the partnership to advance plans to develop AI infrastructure in the state.

Of the US$1 billion earmarked for Sarawak, US$800 million is from SoftBank Group, US$100 million from Grab and US$100 million from PETROS. Meanwhile, SoftBank Group and Grab will invest US$650 million and US$200 million, respectively, for the project in the Peninsula.

The proposed investment will be deployed in stages, subject to projects achieving key development and customer contract milestones, and the necessary closing conditions.

The partnership combines SoftBank Group's global AI and technology capabilities, Grab's digital and AI expertise, and PETROS' local energy and infrastructure development experience.

See also: On a mission to drive higher returns

The collaboration aims to build towards a long-term target of five gigawatts of AI compute capacity and will also explore opportunities across the wider AI value chain, including AI compute and services, advanced technologies, robotics, local workforce and community development.

"The investment forms part of a multi-year plan to develop AI compute capacity in Sarawak, and the parties will also seek additional investors and hyperscaler customers to support the project's development and long-term expansion," according to a joint statement on Monday.

The proposed investment will be deployed in stages subject to projects achieving key development and customer contract milestones, and the necessary closing conditions.

See also: Continuing the journey

SoftBank Group is the majority shareholder of the Sarawak AI project, with an option for Grab to increase its stake in future—reducing SoftBank Group's share while it remains the majority shareholder.

Grab will lead development of the Peninsular Malaysia project as a founding shareholder, with future funding expected through third-party equity and non-recourse project financing.

Given the parties' mutual interest in developing the AI ecosystem in Malaysia, SoftBank Group has agreed in principle to a five-year lock-up in respect of Grab shares that will be held directly by an entity within SoftBank Group, with the lock-up to take effect in accordance with the agreed terms and subject to customary exceptions.

Once fully operational, the facilities are expected to be among the largest AI infrastructure of their kind in Asia, and the project will be developed in close collaboration with Malaysia's federal government and the Sarawak government, aligning with the National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 and Sarawak's Post Covid-19 Development Strategy 2030.

Through the Sarawak Gas Roadmap, PETROS is advancing critical gas infrastructure to strengthen Sarawak's energy security and support its industrial expansion.

As the master developer of the Kuching Low-Carbon Hub, PETROS is also building an integrated low-carbon industrial ecosystem that brings together upstream development, carbon capture solutions, LNG-to-power, downstream processing, industrial parks, gas terminals and deep-sea port infrastructure.

Sarawak's abundant energy resources, established power generation capacity and growing digital economy ambitions provide a strong foundation for the development of large-scale AI infrastructure.

These investments will support Malaysia's ambition to become a regional AI hub, while creating opportunities for Sarawak to diversify its economy and move towards higher-value industries.

title: Stocks climb as buyers step in despite Nvidia woes
article:
(Nov 10) : A renewed wave of dip buying drove stocks to their best day since April in the wake of a technology selloff that had roiled Wall Street, with the market also gaining as oil prices sank.

Following a drawdown in one of the world’s most-crowded trades, a gauge of chipmakers jumped almost 7%. The S&P 500 rose 2.35%. The Nasdaq 100 added 3.4%. That’s despite a 4.3% slump in Nvidia Corp. amid an investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang after his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.

“For now, the market is showing the resilience needed to turn last week’s weakness into another buying opportunity,” said Mark Hackett at Nationwide. “That’s an encouraging sign.”

Also helping sentiment was a drop in energy costs on optimism around efforts to end the Iran war. President Donald Trump struck a more conciliatory tone, saying it’s “highly unlikely” he will order extensive strikes on the Islamic Republic.

That helped reduce anxiety about inflation ahead of a report on consumer prices — the last before the Federal Reserve meeting in December. Still, 10-year Treasuries fell amid gains in riskier assets.

“We continue to see economic conditions as supportive of corporate fundamentals,” said Brock Weimer at Edward Jones. “Thus, we recommend that investors maintain an overweight allocation to equities relative to fixed income.”

See also: Asian stocks brace for selloff as AI rout deepens

The sharp deterioration in momentum that played out in equities last week may have pushed investor pessimism close to peak levels, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas.

The recent tech selloff represented a reset rather than the start of a structural downturn in the AI investment cycle. But the rebound does not remove the risks created by concentrated positioning and elevated expectations, said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

While it’s unlikely last week shut the door on volatility, what unfolded may have been more about investors repositioning within the AI trade rather than abandoning it altogether, noted Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley.

See also: S&P 500 sinks 4% as AI washout rattles Wall Street

“There’s good reason to believe the stock market’s long-term rally is intact, especially given that the selloff overshadowed another week of strong economic data,” he added.
